newsitem.title: USA: SEC chief lauds High Court insider trading stance.
newsitem.headline: SEC chief lauds High Court insider trading stance.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt on Wednesday applauded the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling to uphold one of the federal government's toughest enforcement weapons in fighting insider-trading abuses.
"This decision reaffirms the SEC's efforts to make the stock market fair to all people, whether you're a Wall Street veteran or Main Street newcomer," Levitt said in a statement.

Wall Street's top regulator's comments followed a 6-3 vote Wednesday by the high court, ruling that the government was correct in its interpretation of an important section of the securities law that makes it a crime for a person to use confidential information in securities trading, even if that individual is not technically an insider.
"This decision is a reminder to all investors that insider trading is cheating and will be vigorously prosecuted," Levitt said.

Under the government's theory, if an individual misappropriates secret information and trades on it, it is illegal because the person has breached a trust or duty, even if the individual is not a traditional company insider.

The ruling reinstated the conviction of James O'Hagan, a Minneapolis lawyer whose firm had been retained by the London-based Grand Metropolitan PLC over its 1988 takeover of Pillsbury Co. He was not assigned to the case but, through his position at the firm, he learned of the tender offer and began making purchases.

O'Hagan was convicted of using secret information about the deal to reap a $4.3 million profit in Pillsbury stock and stock options, and was sentenced to 41 months in prison. His conviction had been overturned by a U.S. appeals court.
William McLucas, the SEC's top enforcement official, told Reuters that the court's ruling is a plus for the agency since insider trading abuses account for about 20 percent of the agency's case load.

"You are talking about as much as 20 percent of our total inventory," McLucas said, highlighting the importance court's decision to back the SEC's powers in enforcing insider trading when it involves tender offers.

"This theory has been relied on in a substantial percentage of the cases we have prosecuted. This is indeed a huge victory for the SEC in terms of the weapons available to deal with insider trading in our markets," McLucas said.
He added that the court's ruling offers a "fair measure of guidance."
"These are not people who got technically tripped up on a rule, they committed fraud," McLucas said.
